newsitem.title: USA: Oil drillers down sharply as new capacity looms.
newsitem.headline: Oil drillers down sharply as new capacity looms.

text.p: Stocks of offshore contract drilling companies fell sharply Tuesday as analysts warned investor sentiment had turned against the industry.

Mark Urness at Salomon Brothers said an order placed late last week for new ships from an oil service vessel operator showed offshore drillers were set to start a speculative building programme, which would pressure profit margins.
"With mobile rig orders now totalling 24 units, we believe capacity additions will cast a shadow over the industry, causing many stocks to underperform," he said.
This undermined a sector which had already been hurt Monday and which has fallen 7 percent this year following a quadrupling in stock prices over the past two years.

Urness cut his investment rating on Diamond Offshore Drilling Inc., Falcon Drilling Co. Inc. and Noble Drilling Corp, to "buy" from "strong buy" and ENSCO International Inc, Global Marine Inc. and Marine Drilling Co.s Inc. to "hold" from "buy".
By the close, some stocks had recovered from earlier falls, although they were still heavily represented in the biggest losers on the New York Stock Exchange.
Stocks of the companies with greatest exposure to the shallow waters of the Gulf of Mexico were hardest hit.
Falcon ended the day down $1.25 at $37.525; Noble ended off 37.5 cents at $17; and Pride Petroleum lost 50 cents to $17.375.
Urness said that as the price offshore drillers can charge for their services rises, many will start building in the hope they can capture orders before others can respond.

"Day rates for rigs are going up and the length of contract is increasing. Energy companies would not be negotiating longer contracts if they thought new supply was going to come along and depress prices," said Bear Sterns analyst Russell Hoffman.

Others noted that even if a rise in day rates does kick off the desire to build, there is not enough capacity at shipyards and it is no easy matter to convert from building supply vessels, where margins are better, to rigs.
"When you look at drillers, you see more attrition for rigs than you see additions over the next two years," said Oscar Hernandez, analyst at Lehman Brothers.

Urness noted that even without new building, there is the possibility that oil prices may briefly fall as low as $15-$16 a barrel this year, which would cause companies to abandon ambitious exploration plans and result in rigs being released.
Other analysts say that while a dip in oil prices will hurt oil companies, most are now far more profitable at lower prices due to lower exploration costs.
"What you have to look at is not the raw oil price, but the relationship between the oil price and a company's costs," said Hoffman at Bear Sterns.
